title: Polymarket Users Lost Money Without Clicking Anything. Here’s How
summary:
Polymarket users who had the site open during a short window on October 29 watched their positions get sold and their funds leave their wallets without doing anything themselves. The Polymarket hack did not start inside Polymarket.

It came through a small piece of code from an outside company that loaded on every visit to polymarket.com. The cryptocurrency-based prediction market now says it is returning $3.9 million to affected traders.

How the Polymarket Hack Worked

In a post-mortem published on October 31, Polymarket said a third-party vendor whose performance-monitoring script ran on polymarket.com had been compromised. The attacker swapped the vendor’s legitimate code for a compromised script built specifically to target Polymarket users.

The attacker did not need anyone’s password. For users who had the site open at the time, the malicious script used their active session to sell positions and move funds out of their wallets. Anyone logged in and browsing during that window was exposed. The vendor has publicly confirmed the compromise.

Polymarket’s status page first reported “unauthorized activity affecting user wallets” on October 29 and marked the incident as resolved later that day.

Who Was the Vendor Behind the Polymarket Hack?

Performance-monitoring company DebugBear released its own update on the incident. It said its initial findings point to its domain registrar as the point of entry.

“Our DNS records were compromised through our domain registrar,” the company said on X. “We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain. Based on our initial investigation this attack targeted the website of a specific customer.”

[caption id="attachment_115172" align="aligncenter" width="538"] Source- Twitter[/caption]

DebugBear added that it has “not seen any indication of a compromise of our internal systems,” though it is continuing to investigate.

This is the part of the story that should worry other website operators. According to the statements from both companies, the attacker appears to have gone after a vendor’s domain setup rather than Polymarket’s own systems, and used that position to put malicious code in front of Polymarket’s users. DebugBear’s own internal systems, by its account, show no sign of being breached.

How Polymarket Responded

Polymarket listed the steps it took once the attack was identified:

  • Removed the vendor’s compromised script and cleared every cache.
  • Paused trading and its relayer to stop further drains, then reopened once the site was clean.
  • Reset all active login sessions.
  • Began redeploying third-party scripts with added integrity controls and continuous monitoring, including a stronger content security policy, explicit version pinning and sandboxing.
  • Referred the case to law enforcement while running its own investigation into the threat actor.

The trading pause stopped the bleeding, but it created a second set of losses for traders who were not directly hit by the script.

Where the Polymarket Hack Refunds Stand

Polymarket is returning $3.9 million in total. Of that, $2.7 million covers the initial losses from the attack, and $1.2 million covers losses tied to the hours-long shutdown.

As of its post-mortem, the company said 95% of affected wallets had been refunded in full, through a mix of reimbursements for drained wallets and goodwill payments.

The refunds cover more than drained wallets. Polymarket said it also made goodwill payments in two cases:

  • Positions taken during the attack. If the script moved or force-sold a user’s positions, Polymarket will pay what they were worth when they were taken, including any slippage from the sale.
  • Losses during the trading pause. If a user held a position when trading paused and it lost value because the market ended during the pause, or the user sold right after trading reopened, Polymarket covered the difference from its value at the pause.

Users do not need to file claims or tickets. Polymarket said it identified eligible wallets using on-chain and trading data. Anyone who thinks their amount is wrong, or believes they should have received a payment, can submit a form for the company to recheck.

What Remains Unanswered

Some questions are still open. Neither company has named the threat actor. DebugBear has said the attack targeted a single customer, but its investigation is ongoing, and it still cannot receive email sent to its domain. Polymarket has also not said exactly how many wallets were affected, only that 95% have been made whole.

The incident shows how much trust a website places in every outside script it loads. Polymarket’s own systems were not the entry point, yet its users still lost money, and it took a trading halt, a session reset and a removal of the vendor’s code to stop it.

title: Protecting Cookies with Device Bound Session Credentials
summary:
Posted by Ben Ackerman, Chrome team, Daniel Rubery, Chrome team and Guillaume Ehinger, Google Account Security team

Following our April 2024 announcement, Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) is now entering public availability for Windows users on Chrome 146, and expanding to macOS in an upcoming Chrome release. This project represents a significant step forward in our ongoing efforts to combat session theft, which remains a prevalent threat in the modern security landscape.

Session theft typically occurs when a user inadvertently downloads malware onto their device. Once active, the malware can silently extract existing session cookies from the browser or wait for the user to log in to new accounts, before exfiltrating these tokens to an attacker-controlled server. Infostealer malware families, such as LummaC2, have become increasingly sophisticated at harvesting these credentials. Because cookies often have extended lifetimes, attackers can use them to gain unauthorized access to a user’s accounts without ever needing their passwords; this access is then often bundled, traded, or sold among threat actors.

Crucially, once sophisticated malware has gained access to a machine, it can read the local files and memory where browsers store authentication cookies. As a result, there is no reliable way to prevent cookie exfiltration using software alone on any operating system. Historically, mitigating session theft relied on detecting the stolen credentials after the fact using a complex set of abuse heuristics – a reactive approach that persistent attackers could often circumvent. DBSC fundamentally changes the web's capability to defend against this threat by shifting the paradigm from reactive detection to proactive prevention, ensuring that successfully exfiltrated cookies cannot be used to access users’ accounts.

How DBSC Works

DBSC protects against session theft by cryptographically binding authentication sessions to a specific device. It does this using hardware-backed security modules, such as the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) on Windows and the Secure Enclave on macOS, to generate a unique public/private key pair that cannot be exported from the machine. The issuance of new short-lived session cookies is contingent upon Chrome proving possession of the corresponding private key to the server. Because attackers cannot steal this key, any exfiltrated cookies quickly expire and become useless to those attackers. This design allows large and small websites to upgrade to secure, hardware-bound sessions by adding dedicated registration and refresh endpoints to their backends, while maintaining complete compatibility with their existing front-end. The browser handles the complex cryptography and cookie rotation in the background, allowing the web app to continue using standard cookies for access just as it always has.

Google rolled out an early version of this protocol over the last year. For sessions protected by DBSC, we have observed a significant reduction in session theft since its launch.

An overview of the DBSC protocol showing the interaction between the browser and server.

Private by design

A core tenet of the DBSC architecture is the preservation of user privacy. Each session is backed by a distinct key, preventing websites from using these credentials to correlate a user's activity across different sessions or sites on the same device. Furthermore, the protocol is designed to be lean: it does not leak device identifiers or attestation data to the server beyond the per-session public key required to certify proof of possession. This minimal information exchange ensures DBSC helps secure sessions without enabling cross-site tracking or acting as a device fingerprinting mechanism.

Engagement with the ecosystem

DBSC was designed from the beginning to be an open web standard through the W3C process and adoption by the Web Application Security Working Group. Through this process we partnered with Microsoft to design the standard to ensure it works for the web and got input from many in the industry that are responsible for web security.

Additionally, over the past year, we have also conducted two Origin Trials to ensure DBSC effectively serves the requirements of the broader web community. Many web platforms, including Okta, actively participated in these trials and their own testing and provided essential feedback to ensure the protocol effectively addresses their diverse needs.

If you are a web developer and are looking for a way to secure your users against session theft, refer to our developer guide for implementation details. Additionally, all the details about DBSC can be found on the spec and the corresponding github. Feel free to use the issues page to report bugs or provide feature requests.

Future improvements

As we continue to evolve the DBSC standard, future iterations will focus on increasing support across diverse ecosystems and introducing advanced capabilities tailored for complex enterprise environments. Key areas of ongoing development include:

  • Securing Federated Identity: In modern enterprise environments, Single Sign-On (SSO) is ubiquitous. We are expanding the DBSC protocol to support cross-origin bindings, ensuring that a relying party (RP) session remains continuously bound to the same original device key used by the Identity Provider (IdP). This guarantees that the high-assurance security of the initial device binding is maintained throughout the entire federated login process, creating an unbroken chain of trust.
  • Advanced Registration Capabilities: While DBSC provides robust protection for established cookies, some environments require an even stronger foundation when the session is first created. We are developing mechanisms to bind DBSC sessions to pre-existing, trusted key material rather than generating a new key at sign-in. This advanced capability enables websites to integrate complementary technologies, such as mTLS certificates or hardware security keys, creating a highly secure registration environment.
  • Broader Device Support: We are also actively exploring the potential addition of software-based keys to extend protections to devices without dedicated secure hardware.

title: Hackers Exploit WordPress Flaw Within 48 Hours of Security Patch
summary:
Attackers needed less than two days to start going after a freshly patched WordPress vulnerability. The flaw sits in WordPress core itself, and it can let an attacker run code on a website while that site is installing an update.  WordPress shipped version 7.1.4 on October 28, 2026, to close the hole. Within 48 hours of that release, exploitation attempts were already underway. Security firm Wordfence said it blocked 62,969 attacks aimed at this vulnerability in WordPress over a single 24-hour period.  Anyone running WordPress for a business, a nonprofit, or a healthcare facility is being urged to update right away. 

What WordPress 7.1.4 Fixes Beyond the WordPress Vulnerability 

Version 7.1.4, released on October 28, is mainly a security release. Alongside the critical code execution fix, it patches several stored cross-site scripting (XSS) flaws, a denial-of-service issue, and two separate information leaks.  The update also refreshes WordPress's bundled root certificates after eMudhra revoked its certificates. Of everything in the release, the code execution bug is the one attackers zeroed in on.  Aaron Jorbin, who wrote the release announcement, told users to “update your sites without delay.”  A GitHub security advisory published the next day described the issue as a timing weakness in the update system. If an unauthorized user moves quickly enough while an upgrade is running, they may be able to execute their own code on the server. No CVE number has been assigned to it so far. 

How the Vulnerability in WordPress Works 

When WordPress performs a full-package core update, it first extracts the new files into a dedicated directory inside the upgrade folder. According to the advisory, that directory had a predictable name and was reachable from the public web.  That combination is the problem. An attacker who requests the right file at the right moment, before WordPress finishes cleaning up, could trick the server into running arbitrary PHP code.  Pulling this off is not trivial. The attacker needs four conditions to line up: a full-package update in progress, web access to the temporary folder, a path they can guess, and a short window before the files are deleted. Under controlled conditions, that window may last only a few seconds. 

Which Sites the WordPress Vulnerability Affects 

The advisory lists every WordPress release from 4.7 through 7.1.3 as vulnerable. It also names the fixed version for each branch, including 7.0.8, 6.9.11, 6.8.12 and 5.9.20.  The WordPress project said it backported the patch to all branches still receiving security maintenance, reaching as far back as 4.7. It also stressed that only the newest version is actively supported.  Not every site can be taken over through this bug. The risk rises sharply, however, if an attacker hits a site while it is running a full-package update.  Smaller websites face extra exposure. Many sit on shared servers with default settings, which makes them attractive targets for cybercriminals. 

How Attackers Are Targeting the Vulnerability in WordPress 

Wordfence traced the root cause to full-package upgrades repeatedly using web-accessible paths that are easy to guess. Alex Thomas, a threat analyst at Wordfence, said attackers quickly understood the race condition and turned their attention to it.  Two of the biggest attack sources reportedly kept polling small groups of websites for roughly 14.5 hours. Other sources tried out different folder names and version names.  The pattern looks like large-scale automated guessing rather than attacks on chosen victims. So far, no confirmed reports have put a number on how many sites have actually been compromised. 

How Serious Is This WordPress Vulnerability? 

Sources disagree on how severe the flaw is. The Hacker News gave it a CVSS score of 8.1, which falls in the high range. The GitHub advisory, by contrast, rates it as low severity.  That gap most likely comes down to how hard the bug is to exploit successfully. Even so, the sheer volume of attack attempts and the simplicity of the fix make it sensible to treat this as a serious threat. 

What Comes Next for This Vulnerability in WordPress 

The probing is unlikely to stop soon. Once a vulnerability is patched, the fix itself becomes a detailed roadmap for anyone hunting sites that have not been updated.  The WordPress project says backports to older branches are still in progress. The next major release, WordPress 7.2, is scheduled for December 8.  The advisory credits researcher Umut Bayram with discovering the flaw and reporting it responsibly. There is currently no alternative workaround, so applying the patch is the only fix available.

title: Why Would Anyone Hack a Supermarket Freezer? Europe Is Finding Out
summary:
Supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia were throwing out spoiled food on Monday after their fridges and freezers stopped doing their job. In at least two cases, temperatures had been pushed to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). The apparent supermarket cyberattack came only weeks after attackers took control of cooling equipment in hundreds of stores across France. That raises an obvious question: why are supermarket freezers suddenly a target, and why now?

How the Supermarket Cyberattack Unfolded Across Europe

Sweden saw some of the clearest signs of tampering. ICA Group spokesperson Gustaf Nilsson told the TT news agency that "a limited number" of stores were affected overnight by an incident involving refrigeration systems. One ICA Kvantum store in Sjöbo, in southern Sweden, was more direct. In a Facebook post, it said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius, and that staff were discarding affected products. The Coop chain also reported problems with fridges and freezers at six stores in central Sweden, according to TT, though it did not immediately share details. In Belgium, Delhaize said an "IT incident" had affected refrigeration in several dozen stores, mostly in Belgium and a few in neighbouring Luxembourg. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centers are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores," spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting refrigeration had affected 15 of its more than 700 Belgian stores, and described the impact as "extremely limited. In Ireland, Musgrave Group said refrigeration systems in 13 SuperValu stores were affected by the "cyber incident." Chilled and frozen products were removed from sale as a precaution. By Monday afternoon, the company said the incident had been "fully resolved" and that restocking of chilled and frozen ranges was "well under way." In Estonia, refrigeration technology company Kitman Coldtech said attackers had accessed a computer controlling a client's refrigeration system and raised the temperature to 50 degrees Celsius, public broadcaster ERR reported. Chief executive Jann Mutso declined to name the store but said the attack was addressed within minutes and caused no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain confirmed that one of its outlets was affected.

Is This Supermarket Cyberattack Linked to France?

None of the companies has publicly linked Monday's incidents to France, but the pattern is hard to miss. Last month, attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France. They pushed fridge and freezer temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius. French TV channel BFM reported that the attackers appeared to trigger a forced defrost option, which kept units heating instead of cooling. By morning, tonnes of food had perished. Some equipment had melted, and in some stores the heat had sparked fires. Five of France's major retail groups were hit: E.Leclerc, Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U. At least 300 Intermarché and Netto stores were affected. Coopérative U reported more than 100 stores, Carrefour said 80, and Monoprix said about 5% of its roughly 490 stores were targeted. Bruce Hallas, CEO at Re-thinking the Human Factor, who lives in France, noted on LinkedIn that current estimates sit around 400 stores. He added that some individual branches reported losses of about €250,000. Retailers say millions of euros' worth of food was spoiled, which makes food losses the most visible cost of the attack.

Why the Supermarket Cyberattack Targeted Fridges

The French case offers the strongest clue. The attack did not rely on a new exploit. It targeted ageing systems: internet-connected devices that were still online years after their manufacturer stopped supporting them. Experts say this weakness is common across retail and industry. The cyberattacks in France appeared to target old systems in particular. Timing made the damage worse. In France, the attackers struck while shops were closed, so temperatures kept rising for hours with no one in the store to notice. Monday's incidents in Sweden also happened overnight. Estonia shows the other side of the picture. There, the intrusion was caught within minutes and caused no significant damage. The difference between tonnes of ruined stock and almost no loss came down to how quickly someone noticed.

What We Still Don't Know

Key questions remain open. The reports do not say who is behind the attacks or what they want. The full scale is also unclear. Estimates for France range from around 400 to more than 500 stores, and ICA has not said how many of its Swedish stores were hit. The chains affected on Monday have not confirmed whether their equipment shares the ageing, unsupported setup seen in France. What is clear is that the same tactic has now reached at least five European countries, with fridge temperatures set to 50 degrees Celsius each time.

title: New Android Theft Protection Feature Updates: Smarter, Stronger
summary:
Posted by Nataliya Stanetsky, Fabricio Ferracioli, Elliot Sisteron, Irene Ang of the Android Security Team

Phone theft is more than just losing a device; it's a form of financial fraud that can leave you suddenly vulnerable to personal data and financial theft. That’s why we're committed to providing multi-layered defenses that help protect you before, during, and after a theft attempt.

Today, we're announcing a powerful set of theft protection feature updates that build on our existing protections, designed to give you greater peace of mind by making your device a much harder target for criminals.

Stronger Authentication Safeguards

We've expanded our security to protect you against an even wider range of threats. These updates are now available for Android devices running Android 16+.

More User Control for Failed Authentications: In Android 15, we launched Failed Authentication Lock, a feature that automatically locks the device's screen after excessive failed authentication attempts. This feature is now getting a new dedicated enable/disable toggle in settings, giving you more granular control over your device's security.

Expanding Identity Check to cover more: Early in 2025, we enabled Identity Check for Android 15+, which requires the user to utilize biometrics when performing certain actions outside of trusted places. Later in the year, we extended this safeguard to cover all features and apps that use the Android Biometric Prompt. This means that critical tools that utilize Biometric Prompt, like third-party banking apps and Google Password Manager, now automatically benefit from the additional security of Identity Check.

Stronger Protection Against Screen Lock Guessing: We’re making it much harder for a thief to guess your PIN, pattern, or password by increasing the lockout time after failed attempts. To ensure you aren’t locked out by mistake (by a curious child, for instance), identical incorrect guesses no longer count toward your retry limit.

Enhanced Recovery Tools

We're also enhancing our recovery tools to make them even more helpful. This update is now available for Android devices running Android 10+.

More Control for Remote Lock. Remote Lock (android.com/lock) is a crucial tool that lets you lock your lost or stolen device from any web browser. We are adding a new optional security question/challenge to the process. This helps ensure that only you, the real device owner, can initiate a lock, adding another layer of security to your recovery flow.

Proactive Protection: "Default-On" in Brazil

Keeping our users safe is a top priority, which is why we're working to make theft protection available out-of-the-box for more Android users. For new Android devices activated in Brazil, two of our key theft protection features are now enabled by default:

  • Theft Detection Lock: Uses on-device AI to sense motion and context that may indicate a "snatch-and-run" theft. If a theft attempt is detected, it will quickly lock the device screen to help protect your data.
  • Remote Lock: Allows users to lock their device from any device that provides a web access to android.com/lock without the need to have enabled the feature in advance.

This helps ensure new devices have a critical layer of theft protection from day one.

Continuing To innovate in Device Theft Protection

We’re always evolving our protections to stay one step ahead of thieves. Our ongoing updates help ensure that no matter where you go, you can have greater peace of mind knowing your device and data are protected by Android’s multi-layered defenses. Keep a lookout for even more Android theft protection updates.

title: Android expands pilot for in-call scam protection for financial apps
summary:
Posted by Aden Haussmann, Associate Product Manager and Sumeet Sharma, Play Partnerships Trust & Safety Lead

Android uses the best of Google AI and our advanced security expertise to tackle mobile scams from every angle. Over the last few years, we’ve launched industry-leading features to detect scams and protect users across phone calls, text messages and messaging app chat notifications.

These efforts are making a real difference in the lives of Android users. According to a recent YouGov survey1 commissioned by Google, Android users were 58% more likely than iOS users to report they had not received any scam texts in the prior week2.

But our work doesn’t stop there. Scammers are continuously evolving, using more sophisticated social engineering tactics to trick users into sharing their phone screen while on the phone to visit malicious websites, reveal sensitive information, send funds or download harmful apps. One popular scam involves criminals impersonating banks or other trusted institutions on the phone to try to manipulate victims into sharing their screen in order to reveal banking information or make a financial transfer.

To help combat these types of financial scams, we launched a pilot earlier this year in the UK focused on in-call protections for financial apps.

How the in-call scam protection works on Android

When you launch a participating financial app while screen sharing and on a phone call with a number that is not saved in your contacts, your Android device3 will automatically warn you about the potential dangers and give you the option to end the call and to stop screen sharing with just one tap. The warning includes a 30-second pause period before you’re able to continue, which helps break the ‘spell’ of the scammer's social engineering, disrupting the false sense of urgency and panic commonly used to manipulate you into a scam.

Bringing in-call scam protections to more users on Android

The UK pilot of Android’s in-call scam protections has already helped thousands of users end calls that could have cost them a significant amount of money. Following this success, and alongside recently launched pilots with financial apps in Brazil and India, we’ve now expanded this protection to most major UK banks.

We’ve also started to pilot this protection with more app types, including peer-to-peer (P2P) payment apps. Today, we’re taking the next step in our expansion by rolling out a pilot of this protection in the United States4 with a number of popular fintechs like Cash App and banks, including JPMorganChase.

We are committed to collaborating across the ecosystem to help keep people safe from scams. We look forward to learning from these pilots and bringing these critical safeguards to even more users in the future.

For years, Android has been on the frontlines in the battle against scammers, using the best of Google AI to build proactive, multi-layered protections that can anticipate and block scams before they reach you. Android’s scam defenses protect users around the world from over 10 billion suspected malicious calls and messages every month2. In addition, Google continuously performs safety checks to maintain the integrity of the RCS service. In the past month alone, this ongoing process blocked over 100 million suspicious numbers from using RCS, stopping potential scams before they could even be sent.

To show how our scam protections work in the real world, we asked users and independent security experts to compare how well Android and iOS protect you from these threats. We're also releasing a new report that explains how modern text scams are orchestrated, helping you understand the tactics fraudsters use and how to spot them.

Survey shows Android users’ confidence in scam protections

Google and YouGov3 surveyed 5,000 smartphone users across the U.S., India, and Brazil about their scam experiences. The findings were clear: Android users reported receiving fewer scam texts and felt more confident that their device was keeping them safe.

  • Android users were 58% more likely than iOS users to say they had not received any scam texts in the week prior to the survey. The advantage was even stronger on Pixel, where users were 96% more likely than iPhone owners to report zero scam texts4.
  • At the other end of the spectrum, iOS users were 65% more likely than Android users to report receiving three or more scam texts in a week. The difference became even more pronounced when comparing iPhone to Pixel, with iPhone users 136% more likely to say they had received a heavy volume of scam messages4.
  • Android users were 20% more likely than iOS users to describe their device’s scam protections as “very effective” or “extremely effective.” When comparing Pixel to iPhone, iPhone users were 150% more likely to say their device was not effective at all in stopping mobile fraud.

YouGov study findings on users’ experience with scams on Android and iOS

Security researchers and analysts highlight Android’s AI-driven safeguards against sophisticated scams

In a recent evaluation by Counterpoint Research5, a global technology market research firm, Android smartphones were found to have the most AI-powered protections. The independent study compared the latest Pixel, Samsung, Motorola, and iPhone devices, and found that Android provides comprehensive AI-driven safeguards across ten key protection areas, including email protections, browsing protections, and on-device behavioral protections. By contrast, iOS offered AI-powered protections in only two categories. You can see the full comparison in the visual below.

Counterpoint Research comparison of Android and iOS AI-powered protections

Cybersecurity firm Leviathan Security Group conducted a funded evaluation6 of scam and fraud protection on the iPhone 17, Moto Razr+ 2025, Pixel 10 Pro, and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7. Their analysis found that Android smartphones, led by the Pixel 10 Pro, provide the highest level of default scam and fraud protection.The report particularly noted Android's robust call screening, scam detection, and real-time scam warning authentication capabilities as key differentiators. Taken together, these independent expert assessments conclude that Android’s AI-driven safeguards provide more comprehensive and intelligent protection against mobile scams.

Leviathan Security Group comparison of scam protections across various devices

Why Android users see fewer scams

Android’s proactive protections work across the platform to help you stay ahead of threats with the best of Google AI.

Here’s how they work:

  • Keeping your messages safe: Google Messages automatically filters known spam by analyzing sender reputation and message content, moving suspicious texts directly to your "spam & blocked" folder to keep them out of sight. For more complex threats, Scam Detection uses on-device AI to analyze messages from unknown senders for patterns of conversational scams (like pig butchering) and provide real-time warnings6. This helps secure your privacy while providing a robust shield against text scams. As an extra safeguard, Google Messages also helps block suspicious links in messages that are determined to be spam or scams.
  • Combatting phone call scams: Phone by Google automatically blocks known spam calls so your phone never even rings, while Call Screen5 can answer the call on your behalf to identify fraudsters. If you answer, the protection continues with Scam Detection, which uses on-device AI to provide real-time warnings for suspicious conversational patterns6. This processing is completely ephemeral, meaning no call content is ever saved or leaves your device. Android also helps stop social engineering during the call itself by blocking high-risk actions7 like installing untrusted apps or disabling security settings, and warns you if your screen is being shared unknowingly.

These safeguards are built directly into the core of Android, alongside other features like real-time app scanning in Google Play Protect and enhanced Safe Browsing in Chrome using LLMs. With Android, you can trust that you have intelligent, multi-layered protection against scams working for you.

Android is always evolving to keep you one step ahead of scams

In a world of evolving digital threats, you deserve to feel confident that your phone is keeping you safe. That’s why we use the best of Google AI to build intelligent protections that are always improving and work for you around the clock, so you can connect, browse, and communicate with peace of mind.

title: Accelerating adoption of AI for cybersecurity at DEF CON 33
summary:
Posted by Elie Bursztein and Marianna Tishchenko, Google Privacy, Safety and Security Team

Empowering cyber defenders with AI is critical to tilting the cybersecurity balance back in their favor as they battle cybercriminals and keep users safe. To help accelerate adoption of AI for cybersecurity workflows, we partnered with Airbus at DEF CON 33 to host the GenSec Capture the Flag (CTF), dedicated to human-AI collaboration in cybersecurity. Our goal was to create a fun, interactive environment, where participants across various skill levels could explore how AI can accelerate their daily cybersecurity workflows.



At GenSec CTF, nearly 500 participants successfully completed introductory challenges, with 23% of participants using AI for cybersecurity for the very first time. An overwhelming 85% of all participants found the event useful for learning how AI can be applied to security workflows. This positive feedback highlights that AI-centric CTFs can play a vital role in speeding up AI education and adoption in the security community.


The CTF also offered a valuable opportunity for the community to use Sec-Gemini, Google’s experimental Cybersecurity AI, as an optional assistant available in the UI alongside major LLMs. And we received great feedback on Sec-Gemini, with 77% of respondents saying that they had found Sec-Gemini either “very helpful” or “extremely helpful” in assisting them with solving the challenges.  


We want to thank the DEF CON community for the enthusiastic participation and for making this inaugural event a resounding success. The community feedback during the event has been invaluable for understanding how to improve Sec-Gemini, and we are already incorporating some of the lessons learned into the next iteration. 


We are committed to advancing the AI cybersecurity frontier and will continue working with the community to build tools that help protect people online. Stay tuned as we plan to share more research and key learnings from the CTF with the broader community.

title: Europol Seizes 100+ Servers Running Fake Trading Platforms
summary:
Behind many online trading scams sits a question most victims never think to ask: who built the website they trusted? On 3 November, authorities in seven countries moved against a company suspected of supplying exactly that. The action against an investment fraud scheme with potential victims in more than 50 countries led to the seizure of over 100 servers and the arrest of seven suspects. The operation was led by Germany's Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, with support from Europol and Eurojust. Authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo and North Macedonia took part. They searched 17 locations and seized servers, evidence and assets. The seven suspects were arrested with a view to extradition to Germany. Investigators estimate losses of more than EUR 4 million.

The Investment Fraud Supply Chain

The target was not a single scam group. Investigators say the company supplied fake trading platforms to criminal groups, operating what they describe as a crime-as-a-service model from Cyprus and Israel. Its suspected clients ran fraudulent call centres in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia. Those call centre operators allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. In other words, one business built the storefront, and others did the selling.

How Victims Were Drawn In

The scheme promised large, quick returns from trading in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies or stocks. It started with an advert. The investigation found that affiliate marketing was abused to attract potential victims, with deceptive ads steering people towards fraudulent investment platforms and exploiting their trust in online promotions. The personal data collected this way was then sold to the criminal groups running the call centres. Operators contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities and turned that first flicker of interest into repeated demands for money.

Why Victims Kept Paying in This Investment Fraud

The method relied on making the scam look like it was working. Victims were first encouraged to transfer a small amount. Their online accounts then showed fictitious profits, which made the platform seem credible and the investment successful. Supposed brokers used those fake gains, along with constant psychological pressure, to push victims into sending larger and larger sums. The problem surfaced when victims tried to withdraw. Operators used delaying tactics to block payments. Eventually, contact stopped altogether, and victims were left unable to recover their money.

How a Couple's Complaint Exposed the Network

The case began in 2022, when a German couple reported that they could not withdraw money they had invested through an online trading platform. A first international action day that year led to two arrests and seized evidence. With Europol-supported analysis, investigators identified seven more suspects, including suspected call centre managers. A second action day in 2025 brought further arrests and seizures of money and evidence. Analysis of that material exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, setting up this month's operation. In total, the case took four years to reach the company allegedly behind the platforms.

The Role of Europol and Eurojust

Europol's European Financial and Economic Crime Centre analysed the data, cross-checked it against Europol's databases and brought national investigators together to plan joint action. On the action day, Europol sent experts to Albania and Kosovo to support digital forensic work, and its Virtual Command Post supported the coordinated intervention. Eurojust supported the execution of European Investigation Orders, European Arrest Warrants and freezing orders. Two joint investigation teams were set up at the agency: one involving Albania, Germany and Poland, and another involving Albania and Kosovo. Judicial actions on 3 November were coordinated from Eurojust's headquarters in The Hague.

title: UTA Investigates Suspected Cyberattack After MachForms Service Disruption
summary:
The University of Texas at Arlington is investigating a cybersecurity incident that may have involved unauthorized activity in some of its information technology systems. The suspected UTA cyberattack came to light Thursday, when the university sent a notice to students and employees about the situation.  According to the notice, the incident has affected MachForms, an online form platform the university uses for several purposes, including event registrations, inquiries from prospective students, service requests, and surveys.  The university said it is still working to determine whether the UTA cyberattack has spread to other university systems or disrupted additional operations. 

Timeline of the UTA cyberattack  

Problems first appeared on Oct. 27, when MachForms became temporarily unavailable, according to the university's cybersecurity website. Technicians from the Office of Information Technology began investigating the issue at that time. On Wednesday, the office started corrective measures aimed at restoring services as soon as possible.  Since then, public information has been limited. As of Tuesday night, the cybersecurity website had not posted any updates since Thursday. 

What the University of Texas Is Asking Students and Employees to Do 

The university's email outlined several steps for students and staff to follow while the investigation into the cyberattack on UTA continues.  First, the university asked everyone to follow official guidance from the Office of Information Technology and the Information Security Office, and to pay close attention to university communications.  Second, anyone who notices suspicious activity, such as unusual computer behavior, a suspicious email or anything else that raises cybersecurity concerns, should report it to the Information Security Office at opsec@uta.edu.  Third, students and employees were told not to investigate the incident on their own or circulate unverified information. Questions should be directed to a department head or the Office of Information Technology, and people should rely on official updates for confirmed information. If a journalist reaches out, students and employees are asked to refer them to UTA's media relations team.  Finally, the notice asked the campus community to follow any additional instructions. If action involving passwords, devices, systems, or work practices becomes necessary, students and employees will receive specific guidance through official university channels.  MachForms remains affected for now. Students and employees who need access to the platform for urgent and significant operational needs can contact the Office of Information Technology service desk at uta.edu/help.  The University of Texas at Arlington has not said how long the investigation will take or when full service will be restored.
